questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: first action verify scene safety
questions.text: You arrive at the side of an unresponsive-appearing adult on the floor. According to the AHA Adult 1-Rescuer BLS Sequence, what is your very first step?

answers.text: Begin chest compressions immediately from where you are standing
Verify that the scene is safe before approaching
Apply AED pads before any other action
Move the person to the recovery position

explanations.a: Compressions cannot start until the rescuer has reached the person and confirmed cardiac arrest.
explanations.b: AHA Part 3 makes Step 1 of the Adult 1-Rescuer sequence verifying scene safety so the rescuer does not become an additional victim.
explanations.c: AED pads can only be applied after the rescuer is at the patient's side with the device ready.
explanations.d: Recovery position is for someone who has return of breathing and circulation, not an opening step.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: lone rescuer activate get AED before CPR
questions.text: You confirm an unresponsive adult is not breathing normally and has no pulse. You are alone with a mobile phone. According to AHA Part 3, what is the recommended order of next actions for a lone rescuer at an adult cardiac arrest?

answers.text: Begin 5 cycles of CPR before any activation
Activate the emergency response system on speakerphone, and if an AED is nearby retrieve it, then begin CPR
Drive the person to the hospital before any care
Wait for someone else to arrive before doing anything

explanations.a: The unwitnessed-collapse 5-cycles-first rule applies to pediatric arrests without a mobile device, not adult arrests.
explanations.b: AHA Part 3 directs the lone rescuer at an adult arrest to activate EMS — using a mobile speakerphone if available — and retrieve a nearby AED before starting CPR.
explanations.c: Self-transport delays EMS arrival, defibrillation, and effective CPR.
explanations.d: Waiting for someone else to arrive abandons the patient during a critical window.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: single rescuer 30 to 2 ratio adult
questions.text: When performing CPR alone on an unresponsive adult in cardiac arrest, what compression-to-ventilation ratio does AHA Part 3 specify?

answers.text: 15 compressions to 2 breaths
30 compressions to 2 breaths
5 compressions to 1 breath
100 continuous compressions before any breath

explanations.a: The 15:2 ratio is used for pediatric arrests with 2 rescuers, not adult arrests.
explanations.b: AHA Part 3 specifies 30 compressions to 2 breaths for the single-rescuer adult ratio.
explanations.c: 5:1 is no longer part of any current AHA recommendation.
explanations.d: Continuous compressions without breaths apply only after advanced airway placement, not as the lone-rescuer default.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: skills test correct hand placement compressions barrier
questions.text: The AHA Adult CPR and AED Skills Testing Checklist lists critical descriptors for the testing scenario. Which set of actions appears as critical adult skills test items?

answers.text: Performing compressions over clothing without exposing the chest
Replacing all family members in the room before any care
Correct hand placement on the lower half of the sternum, providing breaths with a barrier device, and minimizing interruptions
Verifying that the AED has not been used in the past year

explanations.a: Compressions are performed on a bare chest when the AED arrives; the testing checklist verifies correct technique, not over-clothing compressions.
explanations.b: Family presence is not part of the skills test critical descriptors.
explanations.c: The AHA Adult CPR and AED Skills Testing Critical Descriptors include correct hand placement on the lower half of the sternum, giving breaths with a barrier device, and minimizing interruptions in compressions.
explanations.d: AED maintenance dates are not on the skills test checklist.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: in hospital scene scenario hallway collapse
questions.text: AHA's in-hospital skills testing scenario describes a person who suddenly collapsed in a hallway. The student is told the scene is safe and to demonstrate their next action. Which initial action does the checklist evaluate?

answers.text: Place the patient in a wheelchair to transport to the unit
Check responsiveness, shout for help, send a coworker for the AED, and assess breathing and pulse
Document the time of collapse on a clipboard
Remove the patient's clothing entirely before approaching

explanations.a: Wheelchair transport during a witnessed collapse delays compressions and is not the AHA-tested action.
explanations.b: The in-hospital scenario evaluates checking responsiveness, shouting for help, sending someone for the AED, and assessing breathing and pulse — the opening sequence of adult BLS.
explanations.c: Documentation is not an immediate-care priority during the skills test.
explanations.d: Full clothing removal is not the first step; the rescuer first assesses the patient.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: second rescuer arrives 30 to 2 continues
questions.text: A second rescuer arrives during your resuscitation of an unresponsive adult. According to AHA Part 3, what compression-to-ventilation ratio do you use for adult 2-rescuer CPR without an advanced airway?

answers.text: It changes to 15 compressions to 2 breaths
It becomes 5 compressions to 2 breaths
It remains at 30 compressions to 2 breaths
It becomes continuous compressions with no breaths

explanations.a: The 15:2 change applies to pediatric arrests with 2 rescuers, not adult arrests.
explanations.b: 5:2 is not part of any current AHA recommendation.
explanations.c: AHA Part 3 confirms the adult ratio remains 30:2 whether 1 or 2 rescuers are working without an advanced airway.
explanations.d: Continuous compressions with breaths every 6 seconds applies only after an advanced airway is in place.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: switch compressors same side seamless
questions.text: AHA Part 5 describes how compressors should switch positions during a sustained adult resuscitation to maintain CPR quality. Which approach matches?

answers.text: Compressors should switch sides every 30 seconds during compressions
The second compressor should take over on the same side as the initial compressor, between cycles every 2 minutes
Compressors switch only after the resuscitation has run 20 minutes
Compressors should change between every breath delivery

explanations.a: Switching every 30 seconds increases pause frequency and lowers CCF.
explanations.b: AHA Part 5 says when switching compressors, the second compressor should take over on the same side as the initial compressor, and for seamless transitions to switch between cycles every 2 minutes.
explanations.c: Waiting 20 minutes for the first switch produces fatigue-related quality drops.
explanations.d: Changing every breath produces dozens of unnecessary pauses per minute.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: second rescuer barrier device pocket mask
questions.text: AHA's adult 2-rescuer skills testing scenario provides a pocket mask once the second rescuer arrives. Which task does the checklist expect this rescuer to perform?

answers.text: Document the resuscitation while the first rescuer continues alone
Provide chest compressions only and skip ventilations
Provide 2 breaths with a barrier device after every 30 compressions
Wait outside the room until ALS arrives

explanations.a: The second rescuer takes an active care role, not a documentation role.
explanations.b: Skipping ventilations contradicts the 30:2 ratio used in adult 2-rescuer BLS without an advanced airway.
explanations.c: The AHA Adult CPR and AED Skills Testing Critical Descriptors include providing 2 breaths with a barrier device after every 30 compressions in the 2-rescuer scenario.
explanations.d: Waiting outside abandons the team and the patient.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: advanced airway 1 breath 6 seconds 10 per minute
questions.text: An ALS team places an endotracheal tube during the resuscitation of an adult. After the advanced airway is in place, how should compressions and breaths be coordinated for the adult?

answers.text: Pause compressions to give 2 breaths every 30 compressions
Provide continuous compressions at 100 to 120 per minute and 1 breath every 6 seconds (10 breaths per minute)
Stop ventilations entirely once an airway is placed
Provide continuous compressions at 60 per minute and 1 breath every 2 seconds

explanations.a: Pausing compressions for breaths defeats the purpose of an advanced airway.
explanations.b: AHA's high-quality CPR component table specifies continuous compressions at 100 to 120 per minute and 1 breath every 6 seconds (10 breaths per minute) for adults with an advanced airway.
explanations.c: Ventilations remain essential after advanced airway placement, just asynchronous with compressions.
explanations.d: 60 per minute is below the AHA-specified compression rate.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: monitor defibrillator role record interruptions
questions.text: AHA Part 5 lists specific responsibilities for the Monitor/Defibrillator on a high-performance adult BLS team. Which item appears in that list?

answers.text: Performs all chest compressions personally
Replaces the Team Leader during every rhythm check
Records the frequency and duration of interruptions in compressions
Provides bag-mask ventilation throughout the code

explanations.a: Compressions are the Compressor's responsibility, not the Monitor/Defibrillator's.
explanations.b: The Team Leader is not replaced for rhythm checks; rhythm analysis is performed without a Team Leader change.
explanations.c: AHA Part 5 lists recording the frequency and duration of interruptions in compressions as a Monitor/Defibrillator responsibility.
explanations.d: Bag-mask ventilation is performed by the assigned Airway/Ventilation rescuer, not the Monitor/Defibrillator.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: minimize pause defibrillation switch airway
questions.text: AHA Part 5 describes when pauses in compressions typically occur during adult 2-rescuer BLS. Which set of events does the manual specifically name?

answers.text: Bystander questions and family conversations only
When the team defibrillates, switches Compressors, and places an advanced airway
Equipment cleaning between cycles
Documentation breaks every 30 seconds

explanations.a: Bystander conversations are not on the AHA-listed pause sources during 2-rescuer BLS.
explanations.b: AHA Part 5 says pauses happen when the team defibrillates, switches Compressors, and places an advanced airway.
explanations.c: Equipment cleaning is not part of the active resuscitation pause sources.
explanations.d: Documentation does not require interrupting compressions.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: puberty signs treat as adult 30 to 2
questions.text: You arrive at a 14-year-old who has clear signs of puberty and no pulse. Which AHA approach should you use for the compression-to-ventilation ratio?

answers.text: Use the pediatric 15:2 ratio because the patient is under 18
Use compressions only and no breaths regardless of training
Use a 5:1 ratio specific to adolescents
Use the adult 30:2 ratio because the patient shows signs of puberty

explanations.a: AHA defines the adult range as starting at puberty, regardless of chronologic age below 18.
explanations.b: Compression-only CPR is an option for untrained lay rescuers but is not the trained-rescuer answer when ventilation skills are available.
explanations.c: There is no adolescent-specific 5:1 ratio in AHA guidance.
explanations.d: AHA Part 6 explicitly directs rescuers to treat children with signs of puberty as adults and use cycles of 30 compressions and 2 breaths.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: 10 breaths per minute advanced airway adult
questions.text: After endotracheal intubation of an adult cardiac arrest patient, the ventilation rate translates to how many breaths per minute according to AHA BLS guidance?

answers.text: 6 breaths per minute
30 breaths per minute
20 breaths per minute
10 breaths per minute

explanations.a: Six per minute is too slow for the recommended adult rate after advanced airway placement.
explanations.b: Thirty breaths per minute would risk hyperventilation and reduced cardiac output during CPR.
explanations.c: Twenty breaths per minute is the pediatric range with an advanced airway, not the adult rate.
explanations.d: One breath every 6 seconds equals 10 breaths per minute, the AHA-recommended rate for an adult with an advanced airway.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: hands only untrained adult lay rescuer
questions.text: An untrained bystander wants to help an adult who has just collapsed in cardiac arrest, but they have never been certified in CPR. What does AHA Part 2 recommend they do?

answers.text: Wait for trained rescuers because untrained help may cause harm
Provide chest compressions only — Hands-Only CPR — for the adult
Attempt mouth-to-mouth breathing only without compressions
Drive the person to the hospital themselves

explanations.a: Waiting without acting is the worst option; even untrained chest compressions improve survival in adult cardiac arrest.
explanations.b: AHA Part 2 says lay rescuers not trained in CPR should at least provide chest compressions — Hands-Only CPR — for teens or adults.
explanations.c: Breaths-only without compressions is not the AHA recommendation for an untrained lay rescuer in adult arrest.
explanations.d: Transporting the person yourself delays EMS arrival, defibrillation, and effective CPR.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: trained BLS provider always include breaths
questions.text: A trained BLS provider arrives at an adult cardiac arrest. Why does AHA Part 3 recommend that a trained provider include breaths in CPR rather than performing compressions only?

answers.text: Because compressions alone never improve survival
Because BLS certification fees require breaths to be performed
Because trained providers can deliver high-quality breaths that improve oxygen delivery, especially as arrest duration extends
Because state law requires breaths in every adult resuscitation

explanations.a: Compressions-only CPR does improve survival in untrained-lay-rescuer scenarios; the issue is that trained providers can do better.
explanations.b: Certification fees do not drive clinical practice.
explanations.c: Trained providers can deliver high-quality breaths that improve oxygen delivery as arrest duration extends, beyond the brief window in which compressions alone may suffice.
explanations.d: State law does not set the BLS ratio; AHA guidelines do.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: 30 compressions count 2 breaths cycle definition
questions.text: AHA Part 3 defines a 'cycle' of adult CPR. Which description matches the manual?

answers.text: 100 compressions followed by 1 breath
15 compressions and 1 breath
5 compressions followed by 5 breaths
30 compressions and 2 breaths

explanations.a: 100 compressions before a breath is not the AHA cycle definition.
explanations.b: 15:1 is not used in any current AHA configuration.
explanations.c: 5:5 is not part of any current AHA recommendation.
explanations.d: AHA Part 3 defines an adult CPR cycle as 30 compressions and 2 breaths.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: breath duration 1 second over volume
questions.text: When delivering 2 rescue breaths during adult 30:2 CPR, AHA Part 1 specifies how each breath should be given. Which combination matches?

answers.text: Each breath delivered as forcefully as possible to overcome resistance
Each breath delivered over 5 seconds at maximum volume
Each breath delivered over 1 second using only enough volume to make the chest rise visibly
Each breath delivered with a measured 1-liter syringe

explanations.a: Forceful breaths cause gastric inflation and may reduce cardiac output.
explanations.b: Five-second maximum-volume breaths cause hyperinflation and gastric inflation.
explanations.c: AHA Part 1 specifies delivering each breath over 1 second using only enough volume to make the chest rise visibly, avoiding excessive ventilation.
explanations.d: BLS does not use exact 1-liter measurements; the visible chest rise is the bedside criterion.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: 100 to 120 per minute universal
questions.text: Your instructor asks the class to recite the AHA-recommended chest compression rate for an adult in cardiac arrest. Which range is correct?

answers.text: 60 to 80 per minute
80 to 100 per minute
140 to 160 per minute
100 to 120 per minute

explanations.a: 60 to 80 per minute is too slow to maintain coronary perfusion pressure during CPR.
explanations.b: 80 to 100 per minute falls below the lower end of the current AHA range.
explanations.c: 140 to 160 per minute is too fast and would reduce diastolic filling between compressions.
explanations.d: AHA's high-quality CPR component table specifies 100 to 120 per minute as the universal compression rate.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: rate too fast diastolic filling shallow
questions.text: A team member is performing compressions at a rate of 150 per minute on an adult patient. The CPR feedback monitor shows declining quality. Which physiologic problem is most likely caused by compressing too fast?

answers.text: Compressions allow the heart to overfill with blood
Compressions become too shallow and the chest fills incompletely between compressions
The brain receives more oxygen than it can use
Compressions automatically synchronize with native heart rhythm

explanations.a: Faster rates do not give the heart more time to fill; they give it less.
explanations.b: Compressing faster than 120 per minute typically reduces depth and shortens the time available for chest recoil and ventricular filling, lowering output.
explanations.c: Excess oxygen delivery is not the failure mode of fast compressions; reduced perfusion is.
explanations.d: External compressions cannot synchronize with native rhythm.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: metronome feedback device pacing
questions.text: A team is preparing equipment for adult cardiac arrest training. Which tool best helps a rescuer maintain the AHA-recommended compression rate during a real resuscitation?

answers.text: A pulse oximeter on the rescuer's finger
A blood pressure cuff used continuously
A metronome or CPR feedback device set to 100 to 120 per minute
A bedside thermometer

explanations.a: A pulse oximeter on the rescuer cannot guide compression rate on the patient.
explanations.b: A blood pressure cuff measures vascular pressure, not compression timing.
explanations.c: A metronome or CPR feedback device pacing the rescuer to 100 to 120 per minute helps maintain the AHA-recommended rate accurately.
explanations.d: Body temperature has no relationship to setting compression timing.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: rate same all ages adult child infant
questions.text: An instructor asks how the recommended compression rate differs between adults, children, and infants in cardiac arrest. According to AHA Part 6, which statement is correct?

answers.text: Adults need 80 to 100 and infants need 140 to 160
Infants need 60 to 80 because they are smaller
Adults need 60 to 80 to avoid rib fractures
The rate is the same — 100 to 120 per minute — for all ages

explanations.a: The AHA does not vary compression rate between adults and infants; the value is universal.
explanations.b: Infants receive the same rate as adults; only the depth and hand technique differ.
explanations.c: Slower rates do not prevent rib fractures and would compromise circulation.
explanations.d: AHA Part 6 calls 100 to 120 per minute the universal rate for compressions in all people who experience cardiac arrest.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: midrange specific 110 per minute coach
questions.text: AHA Part 5 describes how the CPR Coach should communicate compression rate targets to the Compressor in adult resuscitation. Which approach matches?

answers.text: Avoid giving any numerical targets to prevent distraction
Tell the Compressor to compress 'as fast as possible'
State a specific midrange target such as 110 per minute, rather than the broad range of 100 to 120
Wait until after the resuscitation to discuss rate targets

explanations.a: Numerical targets are exactly what the CPR Coach is supposed to provide.
explanations.b: 'As fast as possible' encourages compressing too fast, lowering depth and recoil quality.
explanations.c: AHA Part 5 says the CPR Coach states specific midrange targets — for example, telling the Compressor to compress at 110 per minute rather than between 100 and 120.
explanations.d: Coaching during the code is the entire purpose of the CPR Coach role.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: adult minimum 2 inches 5 cm
questions.text: When performing chest compressions on an adult cardiac arrest patient, what minimum depth does AHA BLS specify?

answers.text: At least 1 inch (2.5 cm)
At least 2 inches (5 cm)
At least 1.5 inches (4 cm)
At least 3 inches (7.5 cm)

explanations.a: One inch is far below the AHA-specified minimum depth for adult compressions.
explanations.b: AHA Part 1's high-quality CPR callout specifies at least 2 inches (5 cm) as the minimum compression depth for adults.
explanations.c: 1.5 inches is the approximate infant depth, not the adult minimum.
explanations.d: Three inches exceeds the upper boundary set by AHA and risks injury without added benefit.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: adult ceiling 2.4 inches 6 cm
questions.text: Your CPR feedback device shows compressions averaging 2.6 inches (6.6 cm) on an adult. Which AHA-specified upper limit are you exceeding?

answers.text: No more than 1.5 inches (4 cm)
No upper limit applies to adult depth
No more than 2.4 inches (6 cm)
No more than 4 inches (10 cm)

explanations.a: 1.5 inches (4 cm) is the infant depth target, not an adult ceiling.
explanations.b: AHA does set an upper limit on adult depth precisely because excessive depth is associated with injury.
explanations.c: AHA Part 1 explicitly caps adult compression depth at no more than 2.4 inches (6 cm).
explanations.d: Four inches would be far above the AHA-specified safe upper limit.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: push hard push fast 2 inches 100 to 120
questions.text: An AHA instructor uses the phrase 'push hard, push fast' when teaching adult chest compressions. Which combination of values does this phrase summarize?

answers.text: At least 4 inches deep at 80 to 100 per minute
At least 1 inch deep at 60 to 80 per minute
At least 2 inches (5 cm) deep at 100 to 120 per minute
At least 2 inches deep at 60 to 80 per minute

explanations.a: 4 inches deep is dangerously beyond the upper depth limit and the rate is below target.
explanations.b: 1 inch deep at 60 to 80 per minute would be both too shallow and too slow per AHA criteria.
explanations.c: AHA Part 1 pairs 'push hard, push fast' with at least 2 inches (5 cm) depth and a rate of 100 to 120 per minute for adults.
explanations.d: While the depth here is acceptable, the rate falls below the AHA-recommended range.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: shallow compressions inadequate cardiac output
questions.text: A new rescuer is performing visibly shallow compressions on an adult, less than an inch deep. Which physiologic consequence does AHA training emphasize when compressions are too shallow?

answers.text: The patient receives too much oxygen at once
Cardiac output and tissue perfusion are inadequate
Recoil time becomes excessive and overfills the heart
The chest cavity ruptures from lack of pressure

explanations.a: Compression depth has no direct effect on oxygen volume delivered.
explanations.b: Shallow compressions fail to generate adequate intrathoracic pressure changes, producing inadequate cardiac output and tissue perfusion.
explanations.c: Shallow compressions are not associated with overfilling; they reduce flow rather than enhance filling.
explanations.d: Lack of pressure does not rupture the chest cavity; the failure mode is poor circulation.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: depth feedback device CPR coach metrics
questions.text: A monitor/defibrillator with CPR feedback shows real-time compression depth during adult resuscitation. AHA Part 5 cites why this feedback matters. Which statement matches?

answers.text: Depth feedback is only useful after the resuscitation ends
Depth feedback eliminates the need for compressions altogether
Visual estimation of CPR quality is often inaccurate, so depth feedback corrects errors a coach cannot see
Depth feedback should be ignored because it distracts the team

explanations.a: Real-time use is the point — debriefing afterwards is a separate purpose.
explanations.b: Depth feedback supports compressions; it does not replace them.
explanations.c: AHA Part 5 says visual assessment of CPR quality is often inaccurate, which is why feedback-device data on depth, rate, and recoil is so useful for the CPR Coach.
explanations.d: AHA actively recommends using feedback-device data, not ignoring it.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.objective: 3.6 Hand placement on the adult chest
questions.keyword: two hands lower half sternum center
questions.text: Where does AHA BLS direct the rescuer to place their hands when performing chest compressions on an adult?

answers.text: One hand directly over the xiphoid process
Two hands on the upper sternum just below the clavicles
One hand on the side of the chest along the ribs
Two hands in the center of the chest, on the lower half of the sternum

explanations.a: Pressing the xiphoid process risks fracturing it and injuring underlying organs.
explanations.b: Compressing the upper sternum near the clavicles produces poor cardiac output.
explanations.c: Lateral placement on the ribs is incorrect and will not generate effective central chest compression.
explanations.d: AHA's high-quality CPR component table specifies 2 hands in the center of the chest, on the lower half of the sternum, for adult compressions.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.objective: 3.6 Hand placement on the adult chest
questions.keyword: heel of hand stacked second hand on top
questions.text: When demonstrating adult chest compressions, an AHA instructor describes correctly stacking the rescuer's hands. Which technique matches the AHA description?

answers.text: Place the heel of one hand on the lower half of the sternum and the heel of the other hand on top of the first
Place both palms flat on the chest with fingers spread across the ribs
Place one fist over the sternum and strike it firmly
Place the fingertips of one hand and the palm of the other on different parts of the chest

explanations.a: AHA describes stacking the heel of one hand on the sternum with the heel of the other hand on top to focus force through a small contact area on the lower sternum.
explanations.b: Flat-palm placement with fingers across the ribs distributes force away from the sternum and reduces compression effectiveness.
explanations.c: A precordial 'thump' or fist strike is not the same as continuous compressions and is not recommended in adult BLS.
explanations.d: Mixed fingertip-and-palm placement does not produce the focused central force AHA describes.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.objective: 3.6 Hand placement on the adult chest
questions.keyword: shoulders over hands arms straight body weight
questions.text: During adult compressions, an instructor coaches you on body mechanics. Which positioning does AHA recommend for the rescuer to deliver effective compressions?

answers.text: Position shoulders directly over the rescuer's hands with arms straight, using body weight
Sit on a stool well below the chest level and pull upward
Stand on one knee and bend the elbows fully on each compression
Lean to the side and push laterally rather than downward

explanations.a: AHA technique places the rescuer's shoulders directly over the hands with arms straight so body weight produces downward force.
explanations.b: Sitting below the chest and pulling upward does not deliver the downward force needed to compress the chest.
explanations.c: Bending the elbows during compressions wastes force and tires the rescuer quickly.
explanations.d: Lateral force does not compress the heart; the force must be directed straight down through the sternum.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.objective: 3.6 Hand placement on the adult chest
questions.keyword: firm flat surface backboard hospital bed
questions.text: An adult collapses on a soft mattress in a hospital bed. According to AHA technique principles for high-quality CPR, what should the team do before or during compressions?

answers.text: Continue compressions on the soft mattress without any modification
Tilt the bed at a 45-degree angle to enhance compressions
Place the patient on a firm, flat surface such as a backboard or the floor
Cover the mattress with extra pillows for cushioning

explanations.a: Soft surfaces absorb compression force and reduce true chest depression even when the rescuer compresses to the right depth.
explanations.b: Tilting the bed does not provide a firmer surface and creates positioning problems for the rescuer.
explanations.c: AHA technique calls for placing the patient on a firm, flat surface so compression force translates into actual chest depression.
explanations.d: Adding pillows further softens the surface, worsening compression effectiveness.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.objective: 3.6 Hand placement on the adult chest
questions.keyword: fingers off ribs interlace lift
questions.text: While performing 2-handed compressions on an adult, the lower hand's fingers are interlaced with the upper hand's fingers and lifted off the chest. Why does AHA technique include this finger position?

answers.text: It looks more professional in training videos
It cools the rescuer's hands during long resuscitations
It allows the rescuer to monitor radial pulse simultaneously
It keeps fingers from pressing on the ribs and concentrates force on the lower sternum

explanations.a: Visual appearance is not the rationale; AHA technique is driven by mechanics.
explanations.b: Hand temperature is unrelated to compression effectiveness.
explanations.c: Pulse monitoring during compressions is not the purpose of finger placement.
explanations.d: Interlacing and lifting the fingers keeps them off the ribs and concentrates downward force on the lower sternum, which is the goal of correct hand placement.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: complete recoil definition no leaning
questions.text: An AHA instructor defines 'complete chest recoil' for the trainees. Which definition matches AHA Part 6?

answers.text: Allowing the chest to fully re-expand between compressions without leaning on it
Compressing one inch more than the previous compression
Holding pressure on the chest at the end of each compression
Lifting the rescuer's hands completely off the chest after each cycle

explanations.a: AHA Part 6 defines chest recoil as re-expansion of the chest after each compression and emphasizes not leaning on the chest between compressions.
explanations.b: Adding extra depth on each compression is unrelated to recoil and would be unsafe.
explanations.c: Holding pressure between compressions is the opposite of recoil and reduces filling.
explanations.d: Lifting hands off the chest entirely between compressions wastes time and is not how recoil is achieved during continuous compressions.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: leaning reduces filling cardiac output
questions.text: A bystander is leaning on the chest between each compression on an adult patient. According to AHA, what physiologic consequence does this produce?

answers.text: It increases venous return to the heart
It improves AED rhythm analysis
It has no effect on cardiac output
It reduces filling of the heart between compressions and lowers blood flow

explanations.a: Leaning prevents the chest from re-expanding fully and lowers, not raises, venous return.
explanations.b: Leaning does not affect AED rhythm analysis.
explanations.c: Leaning measurably degrades CPR quality and is one of the most common errors flagged by feedback devices.
explanations.d: AHA Part 6 explains that incomplete chest recoil reduces the filling of the heart between compressions and reduces blood flow that compressions create.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: compression and recoil times equal
questions.text: AHA Part 6 compares the time spent compressing the chest with the time spent allowing recoil. What is the recommended relationship?

answers.text: Compression time and chest recoil time should be about equal
Compression time should be twice the recoil time
Recoil time should be three times the compression time
Recoil time should be omitted entirely to maintain pressure

explanations.a: AHA Part 6 specifies that chest compression and chest recoil times should be about equal.
explanations.b: Doubling compression time would shorten recoil and reduce ventricular filling.
explanations.c: AHA does not recommend longer recoil than compression; the durations should be balanced.
explanations.d: Eliminating recoil time would prevent ventricular filling and stop blood flow during CPR.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: feedback device alert leaning correct recoil
questions.text: A monitor/defibrillator with CPR feedback alerts the team that the rescuer is leaning on the chest of an adult patient. What is the most appropriate immediate action by the CPR Coach?

answers.text: Direct the rescuer to push faster regardless of recoil
Tell the rescuer to allow the chest to fully recoil between compressions
Add a second rescuer's weight on top of the first
Instruct the rescuer to switch to one-handed compressions

explanations.a: Pushing faster without addressing leaning leaves the underlying problem in place.
explanations.b: AHA Part 5 directs the CPR Coach to give specific feedback to correct quality issues, including telling the rescuer to allow complete recoil between compressions.
explanations.c: Adding more weight worsens leaning and further reduces ventricular filling.
explanations.d: Switching to one-handed compressions for an adult is not the AHA-recommended technique and would not solve the leaning problem.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: recoil allows blood return ventricular filling
questions.text: Why does AHA Part 6 say chest recoil matters during ongoing CPR rather than only at the end of a cycle?

answers.text: It signals the AED to deliver a shock
It clears air from the lungs through the airway
It allows the heart to refill with blood between compressions
It prevents the rescuer's hands from sticking to the skin

explanations.a: AED shock delivery is governed by rhythm analysis, not chest recoil during compressions.
explanations.b: Recoil does not move air through the airway; that requires open-airway ventilation.
explanations.c: AHA Part 6 explains that chest recoil — re-expansion of the chest — allows blood to flow into the heart, refilling the ventricles for the next compression.
explanations.d: Hand-skin contact is unrelated to the physiologic role of recoil.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: less than 10 seconds maximum pause
questions.text: An AHA instructor reviews how long any pause in chest compressions should last during high-quality CPR. What is the AHA-specified maximum interruption duration?

answers.text: Less than 60 seconds
Less than 30 seconds
Up to 2 minutes is acceptable
Less than 10 seconds

explanations.a: A 60-second pause would essentially abandon the CPR effort during that interval.
explanations.b: 30 seconds far exceeds the AHA limit and would significantly reduce coronary perfusion pressure.
explanations.c: Two-minute pauses are reserved for AED rhythm analysis or scheduled team transitions, not as routine interruption duration.
explanations.d: AHA Part 1 and the high-quality CPR component table specify limiting interruptions in chest compressions to less than 10 seconds.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: CCF goal at least 60 percent
questions.text: A debriefer reviews the recorded data from a recent code. Which CCF target does AHA Part 5 recommend that high-performance teams aim for at minimum?

answers.text: At least 60 percent
At least 30 percent
At least 95 percent
There is no recommended CCF target

explanations.a: AHA Part 5 recommends targeting a high CCF of at least 60 percent, with 80 percent often achievable through good teamwork.
explanations.b: 30 percent is well below the AHA-recommended target and reflects poor compression continuity.
explanations.c: 95 percent is unrealistic given mandatory pauses for analysis and rhythm checks.
explanations.d: AHA does specify a CCF target precisely because higher CCF correlates with better survival.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: minimize pre-shock pause defibrillation timing
questions.text: AHA Part 4 cites research about the time between the last compression and shock delivery. Which relationship does that research show?

answers.text: The shorter the gap, the better the chances of ROSC
The longer the gap, the higher the chance of ROSC
The gap has no measurable relationship with outcomes
A standardized 60-second gap is required for the device to charge

explanations.a: AHA Part 4 reports that the shorter the time between the last compression and shock delivery, the better the chances of ROSC.
explanations.b: Longer pre-shock pauses lower the chance of ROSC because coronary perfusion pressure drops rapidly.
explanations.c: Multiple studies establish that this gap measurably affects survival.
explanations.d: AEDs typically charge in seconds; no standardized 60-second gap is required.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: CCF survival 10 percent 11 percent
questions.text: AHA Part 5 cites research on the impact of higher chest compression fractions on cardiac arrest outcomes. Which relationship does the manual report?

answers.text: CCF only matters for in-hospital arrests, not OHCA
CCF should be kept below 50 percent to allow for analysis
CCF has no measurable impact on survival
A 10 percent increase in CCF is roughly equal to an 11 percent increase in survival

explanations.a: Higher CCF improves outcomes in both in-hospital and out-of-hospital settings.
explanations.b: Keeping CCF intentionally low contradicts AHA guidance and lowers survival.
explanations.c: CCF has a strong, documented relationship with survival from cardiac arrest.
explanations.d: AHA Part 5 reports that research shows a 10 percent increase in CCF is roughly equal to an 11 percent increase in survival.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: CPR Coach minimize pauses defib airway switch
questions.text: AHA Part 5 lists situations where the CPR Coach helps minimize the length of pauses in compressions. Which set of events does the manual specifically name?

answers.text: When defibrillation, Compressor switches, and advanced airway placement create the typical pauses that the CPR Coach helps shorten
When the family enters or leaves the room
When the AED battery is being changed
When the rescuer pauses to drink water

explanations.a: AHA Part 5 says pauses happen when the team defibrillates, switches Compressors, and places an advanced airway, and the CPR Coach helps minimize their length.
explanations.b: Family movement is not part of the AHA-listed pause sources.
explanations.c: Battery changes mid-resuscitation are not on the AHA list of expected pauses.
explanations.d: Rescuer hydration breaks are not part of active resuscitation pause sources.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: head tilt chin lift no trauma
questions.text: You need to open the airway of an unresponsive adult who has no signs of trauma. Which maneuver does AHA Part 3 recommend as the standard option?

answers.text: Recovery position
Cricoid pressure
Sniffing reflex
Head tilt-chin lift

explanations.a: The recovery position is for someone with normal breathing, not for opening the airway during CPR.
explanations.b: Cricoid pressure is not used as a routine airway-opening maneuver in BLS.
explanations.c: There is no 'sniffing reflex' technique; the sniffing position describes head positioning in some clinical contexts but is not the BLS airway-opening maneuver.
explanations.d: AHA Part 3 names the head tilt-chin lift as the standard airway-opening maneuver for an unresponsive adult without suspected neck injury.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: jaw thrust suspected spinal injury
questions.text: You arrive at an unresponsive adult who fell from a ladder onto a concrete floor. With suspected neck injury, which airway maneuver does AHA recommend trying first?

answers.text: Aggressive forward neck flexion
Jaw thrust without head extension
Head tilt-chin lift to maximize airway patency
Place the person in the recovery position immediately

explanations.a: Forward neck flexion is contraindicated and not part of any AHA airway maneuver.
explanations.b: AHA recommends the jaw thrust as the first airway maneuver for a person with suspected neck injury because it opens the airway without extending the cervical spine.
explanations.c: Head tilt-chin lift extends the neck and may worsen a spinal injury; AHA reserves it for cases without suspected trauma.
explanations.d: Recovery position is for someone with normal breathing and is not an airway-opening maneuver.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: jaw thrust fail switch head tilt priority
questions.text: You attempt a jaw thrust on an adult with suspected neck injury, but the airway remains obstructed and you cannot ventilate. What does AHA Part 3 instruct you to do next?

answers.text: Continue the jaw thrust indefinitely without an open airway
Switch to a head tilt-chin lift even with suspected spinal injury, because an open airway is the priority
Give compressions only and abandon attempts to ventilate
Place a finger deep in the throat to sweep blindly

explanations.a: Continuing a jaw thrust that does not open the airway leaves the patient without ventilation.
explanations.b: AHA Part 3 explicitly states that if the jaw thrust does not open the airway, the rescuer should use the head tilt-chin lift because an open airway is essential for breaths to be effective.
explanations.c: Abandoning ventilation removes a key component of CPR for cardiac arrest with potential respiratory cause.
explanations.d: Blind finger sweeps are not recommended and risk pushing an obstruction deeper.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: head tilt chin lift technique forehead bony chin
questions.text: An instructor describes the correct technique for performing the head tilt-chin lift on an unresponsive adult. Which set of actions matches the AHA description?

answers.text: Hold the patient's mouth tightly closed while pulling the head sideways
Place both hands behind the neck and lift straight up while pressing the chin against the chest
Place one hand on the forehead and apply gentle pressure to tilt the head back; place the fingers of the other hand under the bony part of the chin to lift it forward
Press both palms onto the cheeks and rotate the face downward

explanations.a: Holding the mouth shut prevents ventilation entirely.
explanations.b: Lifting the neck and pressing the chin to the chest closes rather than opens the airway.
explanations.c: AHA describes one hand on the forehead tilting the head back while fingers of the other hand lift the bony chin forward to open the airway.
explanations.d: Rotating the face downward does not open the airway and may obstruct it.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: no chest rise repeat head tilt before second breath
questions.text: After opening the airway with a head tilt-chin lift and giving a breath, you observe no chest rise. According to AHA Part 8, what is the appropriate next action?

answers.text: Stop attempting breaths and provide compressions only
Press harder during the breath to overcome resistance
Remove the patient's clothing as the first troubleshooting step
Repeat the head tilt-chin lift to reopen the airway and try a breath that makes the chest rise

explanations.a: Skipping breaths entirely after one failed attempt abandons ventilation prematurely; the airway can usually be repositioned.
explanations.b: Forcing harder breaths increases gastric inflation and lung trauma risk without solving an airway position problem.
explanations.c: Clothing removal is not the cause of failed breaths after a head tilt-chin lift attempt.
explanations.d: AHA Part 8 directs the rescuer to repeat the head tilt-chin lift to reopen the airway and try again to give a breath that makes the chest rise.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: open airway required for effective breaths
questions.text: An instructor reviews why the airway must be open before any rescue breath. According to AHA Part 6, what is the basic reason?

answers.text: For breaths to be effective, the airway must be open
An open airway prevents the AED from misreading the rhythm
The airway must be closed to direct air into the stomach
Open airways are only needed if the patient is awake

explanations.a: AHA Part 6 states plainly that for breaths to be effective the airway must be open, which is why head tilt-chin lift or jaw thrust precedes ventilation.
explanations.b: AED rhythm analysis is unrelated to airway position.
explanations.c: Directing air into the stomach is exactly what gastric inflation describes — an unwanted complication, not the goal.
explanations.d: Open airways are most needed when the patient is unresponsive and cannot maintain their own airway.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: pocket mask one way valve back flow
questions.text: You are about to deliver rescue breaths to an unresponsive adult and have a pocket mask available. Which feature of the pocket mask, per the AHA glossary, is most important for the rescuer's safety?

answers.text: A digital display of breath volume
A 1-way valve that prevents back-flow of secretions
A built-in oxygen reservoir
A removable mouthpiece for sharing

explanations.a: Pocket masks are simple devices and do not include digital volume displays.
explanations.b: AHA defines a pocket mask as a face mask with a 1-way valve that prevents back-flow of secretions to the rescuer, the primary protective feature.
explanations.c: An oxygen reservoir improves oxygen delivery but is not the safety feature highlighted in the glossary definition.
explanations.d: Pocket masks are designed for single-rescuer use; mouthpieces are not intended to be shared between rescuers.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: EC clamp seal jaw lift two rescuer
questions.text: A second rescuer arrives with a bag-mask device for an adult resuscitation. Which technique does AHA training describe for one rescuer to hold the mask while another squeezes the bag?

answers.text: Wrap both hands around the bag and let the mask rest loosely on the face
Tape the mask to the face and step away
Use the E-C clamp technique to seal the mask while lifting the jaw
Hold the mask only by its edges with two fingers

explanations.a: Loose mask placement leaks air around the seal and prevents effective ventilation.
explanations.b: Taping the mask is not a recognized BLS technique and would not produce a reliable seal.
explanations.c: AHA describes the E-C clamp technique — fingers form a 'C' around the mask while the remaining fingers form an 'E' lifting the jaw — to maintain a seal during bag-mask ventilation.
explanations.d: Holding by the edges with two fingers does not generate enough force or area for a proper seal.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: supplemental oxygen connect bag mask
questions.text: A respiratory therapist arrives with supplemental oxygen during adult resuscitation. According to AHA Part 8, when should it be connected to the bag-mask device?

answers.text: Connect the bag-mask device to supplemental oxygen when available
Connect oxygen only after ROSC is achieved
Avoid supplemental oxygen during BLS to prevent hyperoxia
Wait for ALS to authorize oxygen administration

explanations.a: AHA Part 8 directs rescuers to connect the bag-mask device to supplemental oxygen when available.
explanations.b: Oxygen is most beneficial during ongoing resuscitation, not only after ROSC.
explanations.c: BLS does not avoid supplemental oxygen; supplementing the bag-mask is recommended when available.
explanations.d: Oxygen administration with bag-mask ventilation is within BLS scope and does not require ALS authorization.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: gastric inflation cause too quick forceful volume
questions.text: AHA Part 8 warns about gastric inflation during ventilation. Which combination of errors most directly causes air to enter the stomach instead of the lungs?

answers.text: Using a pocket mask with a one-way valve
Performing the head tilt-chin lift before each breath
Limiting each breath to 1 second
Giving breaths too quickly, too forcefully, or with too much volume

explanations.a: A pocket mask with a one-way valve is a recommended barrier device, not a cause of gastric inflation.
explanations.b: The head tilt-chin lift opens the airway and helps direct air into the lungs, reducing gastric inflation risk.
explanations.c: One-second breaths are within AHA recommendations and are protective against gastric inflation.
explanations.d: AHA Part 8 explicitly says giving breaths too quickly, too forcefully, or with too much volume causes air to enter the stomach rather than the lungs.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: gastric inflation serious complications
questions.text: Why does AHA Part 8 caution rescuers about gastric inflation during bag-mask ventilation, beyond it being uncomfortable for the patient?

answers.text: Gastric inflation always means the airway is fully obstructed
Gastric inflation prevents the rescuer from continuing compressions
Gastric inflation makes the AED unable to detect a rhythm
Gastric inflation can result in serious complications during resuscitation

explanations.a: Gastric inflation does not equate to a fully obstructed airway; air is reaching the stomach instead of the lungs.
explanations.b: Gastric inflation does not stop compressions, though it complicates the resuscitation.
explanations.c: AED detection is not affected by gastric inflation.
explanations.d: AHA Part 8 warns that gastric inflation can lead to serious complications, which is why technique should be controlled to reduce it.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: barrier device pocket mask face shield bag
questions.text: AHA Part 8 lists the barrier devices that can be used to deliver breaths during BLS. Which set matches?

answers.text: Pocket mask, face shield, or bag-mask device
A bare hand cupped over the mouth
Only a paper towel folded in quarters
Only an endotracheal tube

explanations.a: AHA Part 8 names the pocket mask, face shield, and bag-mask device as the barrier device options for delivering breaths during BLS.
explanations.b: A bare hand is not a barrier device.
explanations.c: Paper does not seal the airway and is not a recognized barrier device.
explanations.d: Endotracheal tubes are advanced airways requiring specialized training, not the BLS barrier options.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: mouth to mouth pinch nose head tilt
questions.text: AHA Part 8 describes mouth-to-mouth breathing for an adult when no barrier device is available. Which set of actions matches the manual's technique?

answers.text: Hold the airway open with a head tilt-chin lift, pinch the nose closed, take a regular breath, seal your lips around the person's mouth, and give a 1-second breath that makes the chest rise
Take the deepest possible breath and exhale forcefully into the mouth
Press the patient's lips closed and blow into the nose only
Tilt the head down and blow under the chin

explanations.a: AHA Part 8 describes holding the airway open with head tilt-chin lift, pinching the nose closed, taking a regular breath, sealing your lips around the person's mouth, and giving a 1-second breath that makes the chest rise.
explanations.b: Maximum-effort breaths cause hyperinflation and gastric inflation.
explanations.c: Mouth-to-nose is a fallback when mouth-to-mouth cannot be performed; the standard adult technique uses the mouth.
explanations.d: Tilting the head down closes the airway; the technique uses head tilt to open it.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: mouth to nose alternative drowning
questions.text: AHA Part 10 describes a drowning rescue where mouth-to-mouth may not be feasible. What alternative does the manual specify?

answers.text: Skip rescue breaths entirely and only provide compressions
Use a pocket mask only — never an alternative airway technique
Push hard on the abdomen to expel water before any breath
If for any reason you cannot give mouth-to-mouth breaths, give mouth-to-nose breaths instead

explanations.a: Skipping breaths entirely is not the AHA-recommended drowning approach where ventilation is critical.
explanations.b: AHA explicitly names mouth-to-nose as an alternative when mouth-to-mouth cannot be performed.
explanations.c: AHA explicitly excludes abdominal thrusts as a water-removal technique in drowning.
explanations.d: AHA Part 10 says if for any reason you cannot give mouth-to-mouth breaths, give mouth-to-nose breaths instead.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: no chest rise repeat head tilt before second
questions.text: While giving mouth-to-mouth breaths to an unresponsive adult, you give the first breath but do not see the chest rise. According to AHA Part 8, what should you do before the second breath?

answers.text: Press much harder on the second attempt
Skip the second breath and resume compressions
Repeat the head tilt-chin lift to reopen the airway
Insert your finger deep into the throat to feel for an obstruction

explanations.a: Pressing harder forces air into the stomach rather than the lungs.
explanations.b: Skipping the second breath abandons the 30:2 cycle.
explanations.c: AHA Part 8 directs the rescuer to repeat the head tilt-chin lift if the chest does not rise on the first breath, then try again to give a breath that makes the chest rise.
explanations.d: Blind finger probing is contraindicated and may push an obstruction deeper.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: lay rescuer no barrier hands only adult
questions.text: An untrained or unwilling lay rescuer encounters an adult cardiac arrest with no barrier device available. AHA recommends what approach for that lay rescuer?

answers.text: Insist on mouth-to-mouth breaths regardless of comfort
Perform Hands-Only CPR — chest compressions only — on the adult per AHA lay rescuer guidance
Walk away to avoid medico-legal risk
Wait silently for EMS without doing anything

explanations.a: AHA does not require breaths from a lay rescuer who is unwilling or untrained.
explanations.b: AHA Part 2 says lay rescuers not trained in CPR — or unwilling to give breaths — should at least provide chest compressions for teens or adults in cardiac arrest.
explanations.c: Walking away abandons the patient at the most critical moment.
explanations.d: Silent waiting deprives the patient of the highest-yield early intervention.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: AED safe pregnancy fetus shock
questions.text: A 30-year-old pregnant woman in her third trimester collapses in cardiac arrest. According to AHA Part 4, how should an AED be used?

answers.text: Do not use an AED during pregnancy because the shock will harm the fetus
Apply pediatric pads to reduce shock energy
Wait until after delivery before any defibrillation
Use the AED for a pregnant person in cardiac arrest as you would for anyone else; the shock will not harm the fetus

explanations.a: Without lifesaving treatment to the pregnant person, the fetus will not likely survive; AEDs are indicated.
explanations.b: Pediatric pads deliver too low a dose for an adult and would not be effective on a pregnant adult.
explanations.c: Cardiac arrest cannot wait for delivery; immediate AED use is the correct approach.
explanations.d: AHA Part 4 says use an AED for a pregnant person in cardiac arrest as you would for anyone else; the shock will not harm the fetus.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: post ROSC pregnant left side blood flow fetus
questions.text: After successful AED-assisted resuscitation of a pregnant person, ROSC is achieved. AHA Part 4 specifies a positioning recommendation post-revival. What is it?

answers.text: Place the person on their left side to improve blood flow to their heart and to the fetus
Place the person flat on their back with no positioning
Place the person face down to reduce reflux risk
Place the person sitting fully upright in a chair

explanations.a: AHA Part 4 says if the pregnant person is revived, place them on their left side to improve blood flow to their heart and therefore to the fetus.
explanations.b: Supine positioning allows the gravid uterus to compress major vessels and reduce blood return to the heart.
explanations.c: Prone positioning blocks the airway and is contraindicated.
explanations.d: Sitting fully upright is not the AHA-recommended post-resuscitation position for a pregnant person.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: LUD lateral uterine displacement aortocaval
questions.text: AHA BLS lists manual lateral uterine displacement (LUD) as a technique used during cardiac arrest in pregnancy. What is the rationale for LUD?

answers.text: It manually moves the gravid uterus to the patient's left to relieve aortocaval compression and improve venous return during compressions
It compresses the uterus to expel the fetus
It replaces chest compressions in pregnancy
It is performed only after ROSC has been achieved

explanations.a: Manual lateral uterine displacement moves the gravid uterus to the patient's left to relieve aortocaval compression and improve venous return to the heart during chest compressions.
explanations.b: LUD is not an obstetric expulsion maneuver; it relieves vascular compression.
explanations.c: Chest compressions continue during LUD; the technique supplements rather than replaces them.
explanations.d: LUD is performed during ongoing CPR, not after ROSC.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: high quality CPR pregnancy same compressions adult
questions.text: When performing chest compressions on a pregnant person in cardiac arrest, AHA's high-quality CPR principles still apply. Which approach matches?

answers.text: Use the standard adult compression rate, depth, recoil, and ratio along with manual lateral uterine displacement
Skip compressions to avoid disturbing the fetus
Use pediatric pad placement and pediatric compression depth
Compress only the upper chest above the breasts

explanations.a: AHA principles for cardiac arrest in pregnancy use the standard adult compression rate, depth, recoil, and ratio, supplemented by manual lateral uterine displacement to relieve aortocaval compression.
explanations.b: Skipping compressions costs both the pregnant person and the fetus their best chance.
explanations.c: Pediatric pad placement and depth are inappropriate for an adult.
explanations.d: Upper-chest compressions do not generate adequate cardiac output; standard lower-sternum hand placement is used.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: tap shoulders shout adult check responsiveness
questions.text: After verifying the scene is safe in an adult arrest scenario, what is the next checklist action in the AHA Adult 1-Rescuer BLS Sequence?

answers.text: Apply AED pads to the unconscious patient
Begin chest compressions immediately without assessment
Tap the shoulders and shout to check for responsiveness
Place the patient in the recovery position

explanations.a: AED pads come after responsiveness is confirmed absent and the rescuer or a bystander has the device ready.
explanations.b: Compressions cannot start before the rescuer confirms the patient is unresponsive and not breathing normally.
explanations.c: AHA Part 3 directs the rescuer to tap the patient's shoulders and shout to check responsiveness as the next step after scene safety.
explanations.d: Recovery position is for someone with normal breathing and pulse, not the next step in the assessment sequence.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: song 100 to 120 beats per minute memory aid
questions.text: A new BLS provider wants a memory aid for the AHA-recommended adult compression rate. Which type of cue most directly matches the target range without exceeding it?

answers.text: A song or beat at approximately 100 to 120 beats per minute
A song at exactly 60 beats per minute
A song at 160 beats per minute or faster
Counting silently with no audible cue

explanations.a: A song or beat falling within 100 to 120 beats per minute matches the AHA-recommended compression rate exactly.
explanations.b: 60 beats per minute would set the rescuer's tempo well below the recommended range.
explanations.c: 160 beats per minute exceeds the upper end of the AHA range and would push compressions too fast.
explanations.d: Silent counting is less reliable than audible pacing for maintaining the recommended rate.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.objective: 3.6 Hand placement on the adult chest
questions.keyword: avoid xiphoid lower sternum landmark
questions.text: AHA Part 3 explains why the lower half of the sternum — and not the xiphoid process — is the correct compression landmark on an adult. Which statement matches?

answers.text: Pressing on the xiphoid process risks fracturing it and injuring underlying organs, while the lower sternum directs force over the heart
The xiphoid process is the strongest part of the chest
There is no anatomic difference between the two locations
The xiphoid is preferred for women and the lower sternum is preferred for men

explanations.a: Compressing on the xiphoid process risks fracturing it and injuring underlying organs; the lower-sternum landmark directs force over the heart safely.
explanations.b: The xiphoid is the smallest, most fragile portion of the sternum, not the strongest.
explanations.c: The two locations differ anatomically and in safety profile.
explanations.d: AHA does not vary hand placement by sex; the landmark is the same for all adults.

questions.name: Adult BLS (1- and 2-Rescuer)
questions.keyword: two rescuer bag mask one mask one bag
questions.text: Two BLS providers are performing 2-rescuer adult CPR with a bag-mask device. AHA Part 8 describes how the responsibilities for the bag-mask divide between them. Which arrangement matches?

answers.text: One rescuer uses both hands to seal the mask and lift the jaw with E-C clamp technique while the second rescuer squeezes the bag
One rescuer holds both the mask and the bag while the second rescuer documents
One rescuer squeezes the bag with both hands while the mask rests loosely on the face
Both rescuers squeeze the bag simultaneously to maximize volume

explanations.a: AHA Part 8 describes the 2-rescuer bag-mask technique with one rescuer using both hands to seal the mask and lift the jaw via E-C clamp, while the second rescuer squeezes the bag, producing a better seal than 1-rescuer use.
explanations.b: Solo handling of mask and bag is the 1-rescuer technique, less effective than 2-rescuer.
explanations.c: Loose mask placement leaks air around the seal.
explanations.d: Two-handed bag squeezing delivers excessive volume and risks gastric inflation.
